summary: An older (tricyclic) antidepressant that mainly boosts norepinephrine and causes fewer dry-mouth-type side effects than other tricyclics, but carries serious heart risks and is very dangerous in overdose. It is mostly kept for depression that hasn't responded to other treatments and for some types of pain, with careful heart and suicide-risk checks.
description: Desipramine is an older (tricyclic, or TCA) antidepressant that mainly blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine, with smaller effects on serotonin. It causes fewer side effects like dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision than some other tricyclics, but it has significant risks: heart problems (slowed electrical signals, irregular rhythm), a deadly overdose from relatively small amounts, seizure risk, and the boxed warning shared by all antidepressants about suicidal thoughts in children, teens and young adults. In mental health care it is usually tried only after other options for major depressive disorder (MDD), sometimes when nerve pain comes along with depression, and rarely for ADHD or depression in children because of safety concerns. Using it safely means careful heart screening, cautious dosing, blood-level checks when available, and close attention to suicide risk.
patient_summary: Desipramine is an older antidepressant (a tricyclic). It works mainly on norepinephrine, a brain chemical involved in mood and energy. It can help with depression and certain pain conditions, but it has important safety issues: it can affect the heart’s rhythm, can be dangerous in overdose, and can worsen suicidal thoughts in some younger people. Because of this, it’s usually used only when newer antidepressants (like SSRIs or SNRIs) haven’t worked. People taking desipramine need regular check-ins, may need heart tests (ECG), and should never change the dose or stop suddenly without talking to their prescriber.

primary.context: Usually tried for depression (MDD) only after SSRIs, SNRIs and other usual first choices haven't worked well enough or caused side effects.

secondary.context: Historic use in pediatric ADHD; currently avoided or reserved for highly selected cases due to sudden death and cardiac risk; not a routine option.

off_label.context: Low-dose TCA for painful diabetic neuropathy; consider in treatment-resistant cases when SNRIs, gabapentinoids, or topical agents are insufficient.
A low-dose option for nerve pain; the pain relief has to be weighed against the heart risks and side effects like dry mouth, constipation and confusion.

therapeutic_response.display: Initial antidepressant effects in ~1–2 weeks; full response often 4–6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.effect: Heart and blood pressure: fast heartbeat, palpitations, dizziness when standing up
common_adverse_effects.notes: Can cause fast heart rate and dizziness when standing. Important to check pulse and blood pressure, especially early in treatment and after dose increases.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble starting to pee
common_adverse_effects.notes: Usually dose-related. Counsel on hydration, bowel regimen, and monitoring for urinary retention.

common_adverse_effects.effect: CNS: sedation, fatigue, dizziness, headache, insomnia, agitation, anxiety
common_adverse_effects.notes: Some patients feel sedated, others feel more activated; dose timing (bedtime vs divided) can be adjusted accordingly.
Weight gain or loss can occur; monitor weight and metabolic parameters periodically.
May lower or raise sex drive, and can interfere with arousal or orgasm. Bring it up with your prescriber, since many people don't mention it on their own.

serious_risks.risk: Heart attack, heart-rhythm problems (including VT/VF), heart block and sudden death (especially in overdose or if you have structural heart disease).
Seizures, which may precede dysrhythmias and sudden death in overdose.
Severe dizziness or fainting when standing up (a big drop in blood pressure) and falls, especially in older adults.
Hepatic injury: elevated LFTs, hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, jaundice.
Agranulocytosis (a dangerous drop in white blood cells that raises infection risk) and other blood problems (low platelets, high eosinophils).

Reactions like a rare emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), and serotonin syndrome when taken with other medicines that raise serotonin (too much serotonin: agitation, fever, shaking, fast heartbeat; get urgent help).
Low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can cause confusion, seizures or falls in older adults.

safety.black_box_warning: In short-term studies, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens and young adults (18–24 years) with depression and other mental health conditions. These studies did not show a higher risk in adults over 24 compared with placebo, and showed a lower risk in adults 65 and older. At any age, watch closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts or unusual changes in behavior, especially in the first 1–2 months and whenever the dose changes. Families and caregivers should watch for these signs and report them to the prescriber right away. Desipramine is not approved for use in children.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to desipramine or formulation components
Concurrent use with MAOIs intended to treat psychiatric disorders or within 14 days of stopping desipramine or the MAOI
Initiation of desipramine in a patient receiving IV methylene blue
Acute recovery phase after myocardial infarction

precautions: Overdose danger: tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are among the most dangerous antidepressants in overdose. They can quickly cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems (QRS widening, VT/VF), low blood pressure and seizures. Prescribers give the smallest practical supply and avoid it in people at high risk of suicide or who have trouble keeping their medicine under control.

Heart risks: heart attack, heart-rhythm problems, heart block and changes in the heart's electrical signals. It needs extreme caution if you have structural heart disease, a past heart attack, a heart-rhythm problem, or a family history of sudden cardiac death. A baseline ECG is strongly recommended for adults, and essential for children and teens if it is considered at all.

Mania or hypomania: like all antidepressants, it can trigger mania or hypomania in bipolar disorder. Before starting, your prescriber will check for bipolar disorder, and an antidepressant on its own should be avoided for bipolar depression.

Seizure risk: makes seizures more likely. The risk is higher if you have a seizure disorder, a head injury, another brain condition, alcohol use disorder, or take other medicines that make seizures more likely.

Dry-mouth-type and blood pressure side effects: although it causes fewer of these than some other tricyclics, desipramine can still cause constipation, trouble peeing, blurred vision, dry mouth, and dizziness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), especially in older adults.

Low blood sodium (hyponatremia): tricyclics can cause this, especially in older adults, people taking water pills (diuretics) and people whose sodium is already low. It can cause confusion, headache or seizures.

Suicidal thoughts and feeling activated: watch for new agitation, irritability, akathisia (a strong inner restlessness), panic attacks, insomnia, hypomania or mania, or new or worse thoughts of suicide, especially in younger people.
Pediatric sudden death risk: Reports of sudden cardiac death in children on desipramine for ADHD; KIDs list recommends avoiding desipramine in ≤18 due to this risk.

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (for psychiatric use) and other strong MAO inhibitors (including linezolid, IV methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: A dangerous spike in blood pressure (hypertensive crisis), serotonin syndrome and severe effects on the brain.
interactions.action: Never take these together. Wait at least 14 days between stopping one and starting the other, in either direction.

interactions.interactant: Other medicines that raise serotonin (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, St John’s wort, tryptophan)
interactions.mechanism: Serotonin syndrome (mental status changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular abnormalities, GI symptoms).
interactions.action: Avoid high-risk combinations; if used together, monitor closely and educate patients on early signs of serotonin toxicity.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that slow how your body breaks down desipramine (for example, paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion, duloxetine, quinidine, some antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Desipramine builds up in the blood, raising the risk of heart problems and side effects affecting the brain.
interactions.action: Use lower desipramine doses, consider TDM, and monitor for toxicity; or choose a non-2D6-inhibiting antidepressant.

interactions.interactant: Other QT/QRS-prolonging or cardiotoxic drugs (eg, certain antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones)
interactions.mechanism: Additive conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia risk.
interactions.action: Avoid combinations in high-risk patients; obtain baseline and follow-up ECGs when co-prescription is unavoidable.

interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression, respiratory compromise, falls, and overdose risk.
interactions.action: Use lowest effective doses of all agents; avoid alcohol; educate about sedation and driving impairment.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: ECG (heart tracing) before starting and from time to time: especially for older adults, people with heart disease or salt-balance (electrolyte) problems, or people taking other medicines that affect heart rhythm.
Vital signs: blood pressure (sitting and standing) and heart rate before starting and while the dose is being raised.
Mental status: Depression severity, suicidality (eg, PHQ-9, C-SSRS), agitation, mania/hypomania, psychosis.
Serum levels: Trough desipramine levels for non-responders, suspected toxicity, nonadherence, or significant interactions; target 100–300 ng/mL.
Laboratory: CBC (if infection signs), electrolytes (including sodium), fasting glucose, and weight/BMI.
Side effects: dry mouth, constipation and confusion, dizziness when standing up, falls, sexual problems, and changes in thinking.

Children or ADHD use: heart rate, blood pressure, and an ECG (optional but often recommended) to check the heart's electrical timing stays within safe limits (PR ≤200 ms, QRS ≤120 ms, corrected QT interval ≤460 ms).

special_populations.pregnancy: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), including desipramine, are not usually tried first in pregnancy, but may be reasonable if you are already stable on it and other options have failed or carry more risk. Untreated depression also carries real risks (early birth, low birth weight, postpartum depression). The lowest dose that works is used, and blood levels may be checked because pregnancy changes how the body handles the medicine. Switching medicines just because of pregnancy is usually avoided if you are stable and doing well.
special_populations.lactation: Desipramine and its active metabolite (2-hydroxydesipramine) are present in breast milk, but infant serum levels are low or undetectable in limited case series. When a TCA is needed in a patient already stable on desipramine, breastfeeding may be acceptable with infant monitoring (sedation, feeding, weight gain). For treatment-naïve breastfeeding patients, SSRIs/SNRIs are generally preferred, but TCAs may be considered if they best match the mother’s treatment history.
special_populations.pediatric: Not recommended as a routine treatment for depression or ADHD in children, because there is little evidence it works and there is a risk of sudden cardiac death. If it is used, it should be only under specialist care, after a full heart check (history, family history, physical exam, usually an ECG), at cautious doses (≤3 mg/kg/day) and with close follow-up.
special_populations.geriatric: Expert guidelines (the Beers Criteria) advise avoiding it if possible at 65 and older, because of dry mouth, constipation and confusion, dizziness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), falls, effects on thinking, and low blood sodium (hyponatremia). If it is truly needed, it is started at a very low dose, raised slowly, with frequent checks for falls and sodium, and regular ECGs.
special_populations.renal_impairment: It is mainly broken down by the liver. Use with caution if you have moderate to severe kidney problems, because breakdown products can build up; the dose is adjusted based on how well it works and how well you tolerate it.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: It is broken down by the liver, so with liver problems lower starting and ongoing doses are used (about 50% lower), raised carefully step by step. Liver tests and, where available, blood levels of the medicine are checked.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic; major substrate of CYP2D6; minor CYP1A2 involvement

dosing.titration: Dosing must be individualized, with low starting doses, slow titration, and careful attention to cardiac and CNS adverse effects. Always consider drug–drug interactions (especially CYP2D6) and patient-specific overdose risk.

sections.heading: Psychiatric Indications & Use Cases
sections.text: Desipramine is a secondary-amine TCA with primary psychiatric use in treatment-resistant unipolar depression. Given its safety profile, it is rarely first-line and should be reserved for carefully selected cases.
items: Major depressive disorder (unipolar), adults: Second-/third-line option after inadequate response to SSRIs/SNRIs, bupropion, mirtazapine, or vortioxetine.
Treatment-resistant depression: Consider as part of a structured TRD algorithm with clear documentation of prior trials and informed consent regarding overdose lethality.
Comorbid neuropathic pain: Low-dose desipramine may be helpful when depression coexists with painful diabetic neuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia.

Pediatric ADHD or depression: Historically used; current practice generally avoids routine use due to sudden cardiac death reports and limited evidence of benefit vs risk. Only consider in exceptional cases under subspecialty care with cardiology input.
off_label: Functional GI pain syndromes (IBS-related pain, functional dyspepsia) at low doses, typically managed in collaboration with gastroenterology

sections.heading: Place in Psychiatric Treatment Algorithms
sections.text:
Today, desipramine is rarely the first medicine tried for depression, because the gap between a helpful and a harmful dose is small, it can harm the heart, and it is very dangerous in overdose. SSRIs and SNRIs have mostly replaced tricyclics as first treatments. Desipramine is mainly used for:

- Depression that hasn't responded to several usual first treatments, when ECT, ketamine or other brain-stimulation options aren't available, aren't wanted or haven't helped enough.
- People who clearly did very well on desipramine before and can be monitored safely (including heart screening and blood-level checks).
- Situations where a norepinephrine-boosting medicine is wanted (for example, marked slowing of movement and thinking, and fatigue) and the heart risk is acceptable.

Because of the overdose danger, it is generally not suitable for people with current suicidal intent, a recent suicide attempt, trouble taking medicines as prescribed, poorly controlled substance use, or limited ability to keep up with monitoring. Many guidelines advise avoiding tricyclics entirely for people at high suicide risk.

sections.heading: Dosing for Psychiatric Use (Adults & Older Adults)
sections.text: Dosing must be individualized, with low starting doses, slow titration, and careful attention to cardiac and CNS adverse effects. Always consider drug–drug interactions (especially CYP2D6) and patient-specific overdose risk.

adult.mdd_initial: 25–50 mg/day PO, typically given once at bedtime or divided BID (eg, 25 mg BID) to improve tolerability.
adult.mdd_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day every 5–7 days based on response and tolerability. Consider slower titration in frail patients or those with cardiac risk.
adult.mdd_maintenance: Usual 100–200 mg/day, once daily or divided BID.
adult.mdd_max: 300 mg/day in severely depressed adults with close monitoring and, ideally, serum level monitoring.
adult.neuropathic_pain_low_dose: 12.5–25 mg QHS, increasing by 12.5–25 mg every several days as tolerated, typically 25–100 mg/day.
adult.discontinuation: If used ≥4 weeks, taper over at least 2–4 weeks; slower (≥4–6 weeks or longer) if high doses, long-term treatment, or prior discontinuation syndrome.

older_adult.mdd_titration: Increase in 10–25 mg increments every ≥1–2 weeks based on tolerability; aim for the lowest effective dose.
older_adult.mdd_maintenance: 25–100 mg/day; rarely >150 mg/day in older adults.
older_adult.mdd_max: 150 mg/day in older adults due to increased sensitivity to cardiac and anticholinergic effects.
older_adult.note: Beers Criteria: TCAs, including desipramine, are potentially inappropriate in ≥65 due to anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, falls, and SIADH/hyponatremia. Consider alternatives whenever possible.

switching.to_from_maoi: Allow ≥14 days washout when switching between desipramine and an MAOI; avoid cross-taper.
switching.general_switching: For most non-MAOI switches, cross-taper over 1–4 weeks depending on discontinuation risk, drug interactions, and clinical urgency. Consider a direct switch only when moving between similar agents with low interaction risk and short prior exposure.

sections.simple_explanation: For adults, start low (25–50 mg at night), increase every week or so, and aim for 100–200 mg/day. In older adults or cardiac risk, start 10–25 mg and titrate cautiously, often not exceeding 100–150 mg/day.

sections.heading: Major Psychiatric & Safety Warnings
sections.highlight: Desipramine is a high-lethality antidepressant in overdose with strong cardiotoxicity and a boxed warning for suicidality in younger patients.
sections.black_box: In short-term studies, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens and young adults (18–24 years) with depression and other mental health conditions. These studies did not show a higher risk in adults over 24 compared with placebo, and showed a lower risk in adults 65 and older. At any age, watch closely for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts or unusual changes in behavior, especially in the first 1–2 months and whenever the dose changes. Families and caregivers should watch for these signs and report them to the prescriber right away. Desipramine is not approved for use in children.
other: Overdose danger: tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are among the most dangerous antidepressants in overdose. They can quickly cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems (QRS widening, VT/VF), low blood pressure and seizures. Prescribers give the smallest practical supply and avoid it in people at high risk of suicide or who have trouble keeping their medicine under control.

Heart risks: heart attack, heart-rhythm problems, heart block and changes in the heart's electrical signals. It needs extreme caution if you have structural heart disease, a past heart attack, a heart-rhythm problem, or a family history of sudden cardiac death. A baseline ECG is strongly recommended for adults, and essential for children and teens if it is considered at all.

Mania/hypomania: As with all antidepressants, may precipitate mania/hypomania in bipolar disorder. Screen for bipolar spectrum illness before initiation and avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression.

Seizure risk: makes seizures more likely. The risk is higher if you have a seizure disorder, a head injury, another brain condition, alcohol use disorder, or take other medicines that make seizures more likely.

Anticholinergic and orthostatic effects: Although relatively less anticholinergic than tertiary TCAs, desipramine can still cause constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, dry mouth, and orthostatic hypotension, particularly in older adults.
SIADH/hyponatremia: TCAs can cause SIADH, especially in older adults and those on diuretics or with low baseline sodium.
Suicidality and behavioral activation: Watch for emergent agitation, irritability, akathisia, panic attacks, insomnia, hypomania/mania, or new/worsening SI, particularly in younger patients.
Pediatric sudden death risk: Reports of sudden cardiac death in children on desipramine for ADHD; KIDs list recommends avoiding desipramine in ≤18 due to this risk.
patient_counseling: Explain that mood improvement is gradual (1–2 weeks for early effects, up to 4–6 weeks for full effect).
Discuss warning signs of suicidality and behavioral activation; instruct patients and families to contact the clinician or emergency services if severe symptoms occur.
Stress that overdose can be fatal; medication should be stored securely and never shared.
Advise patients to stand up slowly to reduce dizziness/falls and to report palpitations, syncope, chest pain, or new shortness of breath immediately.
Review that sudden stopping can cause a withdrawal/discontinuation syndrome; dose changes should be supervised.

sections.heading: Adverse Effects – Psychiatric & Systemic
sections.summary: Desipramine has a broad side effect profile typical of TCAs: anticholinergic effects (though relatively less than tertiary TCAs), cardiovascular effects, CNS changes, metabolic/endocrine changes, and hematologic/hepatic risks.
plain_language_list: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy/retention
Sexual dysfunction (decreased or increased libido, erectile/ejaculatory issues)
Dizziness and falls (particularly in older adults)
Serious but rare: arrhythmias, seizures, liver problems, blood count changes, severe allergic reactions

common.patient_note: Can cause fast heart rate and dizziness when standing. Important to check pulse and blood pressure, especially early in treatment and after dose increases.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic symptoms: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy
common.patient_note: Usually dose-related. Counsel on hydration, bowel regimen, and monitoring for urinary retention.

common.symptom: CNS: sedation, fatigue, dizziness, headache, insomnia, agitation, anxiety
common.patient_note: Some patients feel sedated, others feel more activated; dose timing (bedtime vs divided) can be adjusted accordingly.
Weight gain or loss can occur; monitor weight and metabolic parameters periodically.
May lower or raise sex drive, and can interfere with arousal or orgasm. Bring it up with your prescriber, since many people don't mention it on their own.

serious: Heart attack, heart-rhythm problems (including VT/VF), heart block and sudden death (especially in overdose or if you have structural heart disease).
Seizures, which may precede dysrhythmias and sudden death in overdose.
Severe orthostatic hypotension and falls, particularly in older adults.
Hepatic injury: elevated LFTs, hepatitis, hepatic necrosis, jaundice.
Agranulocytosis and other blood dyscrasias (thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia).
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome–like reactions, serotonin syndrome (with serotonergic co-medications).
SIADH/hyponatremia, with confusion, seizures, or falls in older adults.

sections.heading: Drug–Drug Interactions – Psychiatry-Relevant

items.with: MAOIs (for psychiatric use) and other strong MAO inhibitors (including linezolid, IV methylene blue)
items.risk: Hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome, severe CNS toxicity.
items.action: Contraindicated; maintain at least a 14-day washout when switching either direction.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, St John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.risk: Serotonin syndrome (mental status changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular abnormalities, GI symptoms).
items.action: Avoid high-risk combinations; if used together, monitor closely and educate patients on early signs of serotonin toxicity.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors (eg, paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion, duloxetine, quinidine, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Elevated desipramine plasma levels with increased cardiotoxicity and CNS adverse effects.
items.action: Use lower desipramine doses, consider TDM, and monitor for toxicity; or choose a non-2D6-inhibiting antidepressant.

items.with: Other QT/QRS-prolonging or cardiotoxic drugs (eg, certain antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones)
items.risk: Additive conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia risk.
items.action: Avoid combinations in high-risk patients; obtain baseline and follow-up ECGs when co-prescription is unavoidable.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression, respiratory compromise, falls, and overdose risk.
items.action: Use lowest effective doses of all agents; avoid alcohol; educate about sedation and driving impairment.

sections.intro: Desipramine is primarily a CYP2D6 substrate and has significant clinical interactions with other psychotropics and cardiovascular drugs.

sections.heading: Special Populations (Psychiatric Focus)
sections.text: Use in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults and children is decided person by person, weighing the parent's mental health stability against safety for the baby and the person taking it.
sections.pregnancy: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), including desipramine, are not usually tried first in pregnancy, but may be reasonable if you are already stable on it and other options have failed or carry more risk. Untreated depression also carries real risks (early birth, low birth weight, postpartum depression). The lowest dose that works is used, and blood levels may be checked because pregnancy changes how the body handles the medicine. Switching medicines just because of pregnancy is usually avoided if you are stable and doing well.
sections.lactation: Desipramine and its active metabolite (2-hydroxydesipramine) are present in breast milk, but infant serum levels are low or undetectable in limited case series. When a TCA is needed in a patient already stable on desipramine, breastfeeding may be acceptable with infant monitoring (sedation, feeding, weight gain). For treatment-naïve breastfeeding patients, SSRIs/SNRIs are generally preferred, but TCAs may be considered if they best match the mother’s treatment history.
sections.pediatrics: Not recommended as routine treatment for depression or ADHD due to limited efficacy evidence and risk of sudden cardiac death. If used, restrict to subspecialty care with thorough pre-treatment cardiac evaluation (history, family history, physical exam, usually ECG), conservative dosing (≤3 mg/kg/day), and close monitoring.
sections.geriatrics: Beers Criteria: Avoid if possible in ≥65 due to anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension, falls, cognitive effects, and SIADH/hyponatremia. If absolutely necessary, use very low starting doses, slow titration, frequent fall and sodium monitoring, and regular ECGs.
sections.hepatic: Hepatically metabolized; use reduced initial and maintenance doses (≈50% reduction) and titrate cautiously. Monitor LFTs and consider TDM where available.
sections.renal: Primarily metabolized hepatically; use with caution in moderate-severe renal impairment due to potential metabolite accumulation; adjust based on clinical response and tolerability.

sections.heading: Monitoring in Psychiatric Practice
items: ECG (heart tracing) before starting and from time to time: especially for older adults, people with heart disease or salt-balance (electrolyte) problems, or people taking other medicines that affect heart rhythm.
Vitals: Blood pressure (sitting/standing), heart rate at baseline and during titration.
Mental status: Depression severity, suicidality (eg, PHQ-9, C-SSRS), agitation, mania/hypomania, psychosis.
Serum levels: Trough desipramine levels for non-responders, suspected toxicity, nonadherence, or significant interactions; target 100–300 ng/mL.
Laboratory: CBC (if infection signs), electrolytes (including sodium), fasting glucose, and weight/BMI.
Adverse effects: Anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension, falls, sexual dysfunction, cognitive changes.
Pediatric/ADHD use: Heart rate, BP, optional but often recommended ECG (ensure PR ≤200 ms, QRS ≤120 ms, QTc ≤460 ms).

sections.heading: Formulations & Practical Details
sections.text: Desipramine is available as generic and brand-name tablets.
items: US: Norpramin tablets: 10 mg, 25 mg; generic desipramine tablets: 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150 mg.
Administration: Oral; can be given with food to reduce GI upset; typically dosed once nightly or divided BID.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action – Psychiatric Relevance
sections.text: Desipramine predominantly inhibits norepinephrine reuptake at the presynaptic terminal, increasing synaptic NE availability. It has lesser effects on serotonin than tertiary TCAs. Over time, TCAs also desensitize adenyl cyclase and downregulate beta-adrenergic and certain serotonin receptors. This noradrenergic profile can be useful for psychomotor retardation, low energy, and impaired concentration but also increases risk of tachycardia, hypertension, and anxiety/activation in some patients.

faqs.q: When should I consider desipramine instead of an SSRI or SNRI?
faqs.a: Mainly for depression that hasn't responded to several of the usual first treatments, when your suicide risk and heart risk are relatively low, or when you clearly did very well on desipramine in the past. It may also be considered when nerve pain that comes with depression is a major concern and other medicines haven't helped enough.

faqs.q: How do I manage suicide risk when prescribing desipramine?
faqs.a: Assess baseline suicide risk (history of attempts, current ideation, access to means), avoid TCAs in high-risk patients, prescribe small quantities with frequent follow-up (especially in the first 1–2 months and after dose changes), involve family when possible, and provide clear emergency instructions. Consider an alternative antidepressant with lower overdose lethality if risk is moderate or high.

faqs.q: Do I need an ECG before starting desipramine?
faqs.a: An ECG is strongly recommended for adults and essential for older adults or anyone with heart risk factors (a personal or family history of heart-rhythm problems, fainting, or structural heart disease). For children and teens, a full heart check (including thinking about an ECG) is recommended if desipramine is ever considered.

faqs.q: How do I taper desipramine to minimize discontinuation symptoms?
faqs.a: After at least 4 weeks of treatment, taper gradually over 2–4 weeks, or longer (4–6+ weeks) after high doses or long-term use. If significant withdrawal symptoms emerge (eg, flu-like symptoms, sleep disturbance, agitation), return to the prior dose and decrease more slowly.

faqs.q: Is desipramine appropriate in bipolar depression?
faqs.a: No, not on its own. Tricyclics can trigger mania or rapid mood cycling and are generally avoided in bipolar depression. If used at all, it should only be together with a mood stabilizer, and usually only when other treatments have failed, under specialist care.
